title: Harvest and House
premise: Urban explorer Xanthe Reyes returns to her decaying hometown of Marrow Creek to map a network of tunnels that appear on no survey, only to find her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on her mother's porch—unchanged after twenty years. Wren is the last guardian of a founders' ritual that keeps something in the old well asleep, and the ritual was left unfinished when the town's children scattered. As neighbors who 'stayed' begin losing their memories and their faces, Xanthe must gather the descendants of the founding families—including the man who wronged her family—to complete the rite before the well refills on the equinox. She succeeds at terrible cost: Wren is unmade in the process, but the found family Xanthe assembles chooses to stay and become the town's new keepers, trading invisibility for belonging.
about_author: Silas Sandoval is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing records for towns that no longer exist. They write horror about places that remember people better than people remember themselves.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Returning to Marrow Creek after her mother's funeral, she finds Wren—the imaginary friend of her childhood—sitting on the porch, unchanged. The beat is uncanny dread braided with grief; documentation becomes her defense against believing.

chapters.title: Maps That Lie
chapters.summary: Xanthe surveys the town with lidar and old plat books, discovering tunnels beneath every foundation that no survey records. POV alternates with journal excerpts from founder Abigail Crane. Beat: intellectual fascination curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Wren Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Wren speaks only in things Xanthe said as a child, replaying them back like evidence. She tests whether Wren is hallucination, hoax, or haunting—and fails all three tests. Beat: the terror of being known completely.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Xanthe interviews remaining residents: Pastor Ellery, diner owner Mabel Cho, and hollow-eyed Deputy Fenn, whose faces seem subtly wrong in photographs. Beat: loneliness meeting its mirror in a town full of people nobody left for.

chapters.title: What the Well Wants
chapters.summary: In the courthouse basement, Xanthe finds the founders' covenant: a ritual requiring seven descendants, performed each generation, or the well 'refills.' The last rite was abandoned in 2004—the year her family fled. Beat: guilt reframed as inheritance.

chapters.title: Tunnel Music
chapters.summary: Night exploration POV. Deep in the tunnels, Xanthe hears singing that harmonizes with her own breathing and finds her mother's handwriting on walls her mother never entered. Beat: the past is not behind her; it is below her.

chapters.title: Fenn's Confession
chapters.summary: Deputy Fenn admits the police have been feeding missing-persons reports into the well for decades—a justice outside any law, he calls it. He begs Xanthe not to finish the ritual, because finishing means judgment. Beat: complicity wearing a badge.

chapters.title: Seven Names
chapters.summary: Xanthe compiles the descendant list and discovers she is one of the seven—and that Wren has been protecting her name since childhood. Beat: the imaginary friend was real insurance all along.

chapters.title: Mabel's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Mabel Cho loses her memories overnight, smiling blankly at her own diner. The forgetting spreads through those who stayed. Xanthe realizes the well isn't waiting—it's already drinking. Beat: urgency replaces dread.

chapters.title: The Boy Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter, young Xanthe's POV, revealing how Wren first appeared the night her father disappeared into the tunnels—and what her mother made her promise to forget. Beat: memory as both wound and shield.

chapters.title: Recruiting Ghosts
chapters.summary: Xanthe tracks down scattered descendants: a hospice nurse in Ohio, an incarcerated man named Dill Crane, a runaway teen with the right bloodline. Each refuses until shown the tunnel maps. Beat: building a found family out of obligation and reluctant hope.

chapters.title: Dill Crane, From Inside
chapters.summary: Dill's POV from prison—he has dreamed of the well every night of his sentence and knows things the archives don't. He agrees to help if they bring him home, dead or alive. Beat: a criminal offering the most honest terms of anyone.

chapters.title: The Refilling Begins
chapters.summary: Water rises in dry wells across town; basements flood with something warm that whispers names. Pastor Ellery's congregation forgets him mid-sermon. Beat: the deadline stops being theoretical.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren reveals the ritual's true cost: a seventh participant must be given wholly to the well, and guardians like Wren exist only to be spent. Wren volunteers. Xanthe refuses to accept. Beat: love against sacrifice.

chapters.title: Breaking Into the Archive of Faces
chapters.summary: The team raids the flooded courthouse to recover the original rite, navigating drowned halls where the forgotten townsfolk stand motionless, faceless, holding lanterns. Beat: awe and horror fused; the stakes made visible.

chapters.title: Ellery's Heresy
chapters.summary: Pastor Ellery, half-forgotten himself, tries to stop them: he believes the well is mercy, erasing pain, and the town should let it refill. Fenn turns his gun on the group—or on Ellery. Beat: ideology versus survival, trust fracturing.

chapters.title: Descent of Seven
chapters.summary: Six descendants plus Wren descend through the singing tunnels to the well chamber, following Abigail Crane's instructions while the water rises around their ankles. Beat: commitment; no road back up.

chapters.title: The First Circle
chapters.summary: The rite begins. Each descendant must surrender a true memory to seal a boundary—Xanthe gives up her father's face, Dill gives his daughter's laugh. The well pushes back with offers instead of demands. Beat: temptation as the sharpest blade.

chapters.title: What Took My Father
chapters.summary: At the final seal, the well shows Xanthe the truth: her father stayed voluntarily, becoming a keeper, and Wren was his parting gift to her. Beat: grief transmuted into understanding; fury at everyone, including herself.

chapters.title: Equinox, Rising Water
chapters.summary: Climax. Ellery sabotages the circle to hasten the refilling; the chamber floods; Fenn drowns holding the line open. With six seals set and no seventh volunteer, Xanthe must choose between Wren's sacrifice and a broken rite. Beat: everything converges at once.

chapters.title: The Unmaking of Wren
chapters.summary: Resolution of the climax: Xanthe performs the seventh seal using Wren herself—but by consent, speaking Wren's true name, which she finally remembers. The well sleeps. Wren dissolves saying thank you. Beat: devastating tenderness; the price paid knowingly.

chapters.title: Keepers of Marrow Creek
chapters.summary: Epilogue, one year later. The survivors remain—not trapped, but chosen—as the town's new keepers, teaching the rite to the runaway teen. On the porch, a porch light burns for Wren. Xanthe documents everything still, because now the record is a promise. Beat: found family, quiet justice, earned peace.
